Diesel to Surcharge

Most freight contracts add a fuel surcharge that moves with the U.S. Energy Information Administration's (EIA) weekly diesel price. Enter a diesel price to see how large the surcharge gets, and what share of the freight bill it becomes, for a truckload, LTL, and rail shipment.

From the freight bill to the store shelf

Freight is only one part of what goods cost. Counting every trip from farm or mine to factory, warehouse, and store, for-hire trucking and rail make up about 7% of what retailers pay for the goods they sell, and about 2% of all consumer spending, based on the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) 2023 input-output tables. If the whole fuel-driven freight increase is passed along, prices would change by about:

The consumer goods range depends on how stores pass along the cost. The low end adds the higher freight cost dollar for dollar. The high end assumes stores keep the same percentage markup. These figures count only the freight channel. They leave out private truck fleets that shippers run themselves and parcel carriers, which also pay more for fuel, so the real effect is likely larger. They also leave out what consumers pay directly for gasoline and diesel.

How these contracts work

Truckload: cents per mile

The contract sets a base diesel price, often near $1.20 to $1.25, and an assumed fuel economy, often 6 miles per gallon. Each week the surcharge per mile equals the EIA price minus the base price, divided by the miles per gallon. The shipper pays that on top of the per-mile base rate.

LTL: percent of the base rate

Less-than-truckload (LTL) carriers publish a table. For each price step above a base price, the surcharge goes up a set number of percentage points. That percentage is applied to the shipment's base charge after any discount. Most tables update weekly with the EIA price.

Rail: monthly, with a lag

Large railroads mostly use the same EIA diesel price, but average it over a month and apply it about two months later. Union Pacific says in its 10-K that changing fuel prices can take up to two months to affect its surcharge. That lag is why rail rates move later than truck rates.

Diesel prices: EIA weekly U.S. No. 2 diesel retail price, all types (via FRED, series GASDESW), through . Reported shares: fuel surcharge revenue divided by the matching revenue total, from each carrier's 10-K filings. Truckload: Heartland, Knight-Swift, Marten, Werner. LTL: Old Dominion, Saia, XPO (LTL segment). Rail: Union Pacific, Norfolk Southern.
Assumptions: Truckload base rate $2.50 a mile, base diesel price $1.25, 6 miles per gallon, 800-mile trip. LTL surcharge adds 0.35% of the base charge for each 5¢ above $1.15, on a $400 shipment. Rail surcharge adds 0.25% of the base charge for each 4¢ above $1.90, on a $3,000 carload, with a two-month lag. These are round numbers set so results land near what public carriers report, not any one carrier's table.
Freight shares: BEA 2023 commodity-by-commodity total requirements and use tables (summary level), truck transportation (484) and rail transportation (482) content of personal consumption expenditures.
This is an educational tool. Real contracts differ in base prices, steps, rounding, caps, and which week's price applies. The weekly history holds base rates fixed at the assumptions above, so it shows only the effect of diesel prices.
